Author: Dwivedi, Lavkesh
Title: When Agents Call Agents: Failure Propagation Patterns in Multi-Model Agentic Pipelines
Abstract Note: In multi-agent LLM pipelines, model changes at one agent routinely produce failures at others: a provider deprecation cascades through every agent sharing the affected endpoint (Groq/crewAI, January 2025), schema migrations break downstream parsers when agents update on different schedules (OpenAI functions-to-tools, November 2023), and silent behavioral drift poisons the context consumed by downstream agents (Anthropic April 2026). In each case, the root cause is in one place; the observable failure is in another. This decoupling is the attribution gap: a structural property of any architecture in which one agent's output is another agent's input, not an implementation deficiency that better tooling will close. An empirical study of 1,600 annotated execution traces across seven production frameworks confirms that inter-agent coordination failures-not base model capability limits-are the primary failure surface in multi-agent LLM systems (Cemri et al., 2025). This paper characterizes four pipeline architectures with distinct propagation topologies, six failure propagation modes grounded in documented production incidents and peer-reviewed empirical studies, and five engineering patterns for constraining propagation across agent boundaries. The patterns address different points in the propagation chain: interagent behavioral contracts validate agent-to-agent interfaces before traffic promotion; typed agent boundaries with schema versioning detect schema cascade failures at the handoff point; propagationaware circuit breakers coordinate failure response across agent boundaries; homogeneous model version pinning eliminates within-pipeline model heterogeneity as a root cause class; and orchestrator health telemetry provides the attribution path from observable failures back to originating agents. Pseudocode implementations and implementation tradeoff analysis are provided for each pattern.

Author: Owolabi, Saviour
Title: LLM-SATD: An Empirical Study of Self-Admitted Technical Debt in Software Integrating Large Language Models
Abstract Note: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software systems to support capabili-ties such as task automation and conversational interfaces. Under pressure to rapidly ship LLM-powered features and gain first-mover advantage, developers may incur technical debt: workarounds and shortcuts that accelerate short-term delivery but make future software maintenance and evolution more difficult. Developers often acknowledge such debt in code comments, forming Self-Admitted Technical Debt (SATD). These comments capture the maintenance challenges developers face. SATD has therefore been studied both in general software systems and in specialized contexts such as machine-learning systems, revealing concerns such as data-pipeline management as drivers of SATD. However, despite the rapid adoption of LLMs, empirical evidence on SATD arising specifically from LLM integration, which we call LLM-SATD, remains scarce. To address this gap, we empirically study open-source projects to determine the prevalence of LLM-SATD, the effort required to repay it, and its recurring forms. We construct a dataset of 90,845 SATD instances mined from 2,854 GitHub repositories and develop an approach to identify LLM-SATD among them. We find that LLM-SATD accounts for 5.6% of all SATD (5,086 comments). It is also repaid more often than non-LLM-SATD (62.3% vs. 46.3%) and requires less effort to repay: at the median, 32.6% fewer modified lines of code, 37.5% fewer modified files, and 6.9% fewer Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) modifications, while taking nearly the same time. Through thematic analysis, we derive a taxonomy of LLM-SATD with 22 subcategories across 10 categories, capturing challenges specific to LLM integration, such as Agent Integration Debt and Prompt Debt. We further examine repayment time and effort across LLM-SATD categories, finding Testing and Behaviour Verification Debt particularly concerning, with a median repayment time of 76.6 days and a median of 179 modified lines. We also find that LLM-SATD activity is largely maintainer-driven: maintainers introduce 87.1% and repay 86.9% of LLM-SATD. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to reduce LLM-SATD and streamline repayment, helping practitioners estimate the maintenance effort involved in building LLM-based features and prioritize debts to address early.

Author: de Sousa Job, Ricardo
Title: Understanding platform-specific code
Abstract Note: Código específico de plataforma refere-se a código que adapta seu comportamento de acordo com a plataforma de execução. Sistemas de software modernos são desenvolvidos e testados em múltiplas plataformas, exigindo que desenvolvedores lidem com diferentes sistemas operacionais e ambientes de execução. Nesse contexto, o uso de código específico de plataforma torna-se necessário, seja para adaptar o comportamento do sistema, seja para tratar operações indisponíveis, introduzindo benefícios e desafios para o desenvolvimento e teste de software. Apesar de sua relevância prática, há carência de soluções que apoiem a compreensão sistemática de seu uso. Além disso, o código específico de plataforma permanece pouco explorado na literatura de engenharia de software, especialmente quanto à sua prevalência, estratégias de implementação e impacto. O objetivo desta tese é analisar e avaliar o uso de código específico de plataforma em código de produção e de teste. Para isso, realizamos uma investigação empírica no ecossistema Python. A pesquisa é estruturada em quatro unidades principais. Inicialmente, propomos o conceito de código específico de plataforma e caracterizamos APIs específicas de plataforma, analisando sua disponibilidade e uso na prática. Em seguida, investigamos testes específicos de sistema operacional, examinando sua relação com test smells, flaky tests e desafios de teste em múltiplas plataformas. Posteriormente, conduzimos um estudo de caso na biblioteca padrão do Python para compreender como esse tipo de código é implementado e sua relação com código defensivo e problemas de segurança. Por fim, desenvolvemos PSASpotter, uma ferramenta para detectar e analisar código específico de plataforma, viabilizando estudos em larga escala e aplicações práticas. Os resultados mostram que o código específico de plataforma é amplamente utilizado, mas frequentemente carece de documentação, boas práticas e anti-padrões. Também identificamos relações com test smells, flaky tests e desafios de teste em múltiplas plataformas, além de associações com issues e problemas de segurança. Como contribuição, esta tese apresenta novas abstrações, evidências empíricas, ferramentas e datasets, avançando a compreensão do desenvolvimento e teste de software em múltiplas plataformas e apoiando pesquisadores e profissionais na gestão desse tipo de código.

Author: Elizondo Solano, Andrey M.
Title: Orchestration spaces in inter-organizational developments of information infrastructures: early orchestration of a large-scale regional interoperability infrastructure in NHS England
Abstract Note: This study addresses the phenomenon of orchestration, defined as the long-term mobilization, convergence, and arrangement of actors in the development of an inter-organizational information system for integrating and sharing data across a regional care ecosystem in England. Using multi-sited longitudinal qualitative research, I analyze the first five years (2014–2019) of a novel, regional interoperability platform in England’s National Health Service (NHS), intended to interconnect primary, secondary, and social care information systems for the integration and exchange of clinical data. This region was an early mover in the implementation of new policies to promote integrated care and information systems interoperability at regional level. Experiences like the National Programme for Information Technology (NPfIT)(2002–2011) in NHS England have demonstrated that the scale and complexity of the NHS make the implementation of one-size-fits-all, nation-wide, centralized digital solutions difficult. After NPfIT was abandoned in 2011, hospitals were free to choose and implement the Electronic Medical Records (EMR) system they believed best matched their requirements. Diverse stand-alone computer systems were thus implemented under this laissez-faire policy. This has contributed to the separate digitalization of primary, secondary, and social care services and reinforced the fragmentation and dispersion of data. Since 2014, increasing priority has been given to integrating care, with health policies emphasizing the efficient processing of patients and patient data, and integrating information to support entire care pathways. This has created a new impetus to bring previously separated systems together through shared information infrastructures. Avoiding nationwide projects, such efforts have been promoted through region-wide approaches initiated and governed by participant organizations. Heterogenous groups of autonomous organizations must mobilize over the long-term to develop–conceptualize, design, implement, adopt, and post-implement–an inter-organizational digital infrastructure. These efforts towards information systems interoperability at regional level, present a challenging sociotechnical dynamic. In these long-term constructions of digital information infrastructures, governance is neither top-down nor bottom-up, participation is not mandated, and the roles of the organizations involved are unclarified. Development is shaped by in-the-making design and use, the multiplicity of agendas, contexts, and user bases, the installed base, and existing systems and practices that restrict design scope. At the inter-organizational level, the process also involves links between subsystems, a diversity of actors, a dispersion of knowledge, and diverse and asymmetrical installed bases. In situations such as these, involving autonomous and interrelated organizations and where knowledge and authority do not rest on a single actor, long-term mobilization and participation become critical, and traditional command and control dynamics are ineffective. Therefore, stakeholders are required to find ways to coordinate in a non-hierarchical manner. My research contributes to an understanding of orchestration in the development of a novel, inter-organizational information infrastructure, within a context where authority, knowledge, and expertise do not lie in a single entity or person.

Author: Iho, Albert
Title: PRICE ANOMALY DETECTION IN NORDIC E-COMMERCE USING STATISTICAL AND UNSUPERVISED MACHINE LEARNING METHODS
Abstract Note:
E-commerce price monitoring systems depend on timely and reliable competitorpricing data, but the collected price records may contain both statistical outliers and deterministic data-quality errors. This thesis investigates anomaly detection methods for competitor-pricing data under practical business and deployment constraints. The study compares statistical detectors, unsupervised forest-based detectors, and rule-based sanity checks, with the aim of identifying a detector configuration suitable
for a layered detection system. The evaluated statistical methods include the standard z-score, modified z-scores based on MAD and Sn, and hybrid robust z-score variants. The unsupervised methods include Isolation Forest, Extended Isolation Forest, and Robust Random Cut Forest. Because complete ground-truth anomaly labels are not available, the evaluation uses a reproducible synthetic anomaly injection protocol covering multiple anomaly cases, including price spikes, price drops, decimal shifts, currency swaps, zero prices, negative prices, and list-price violations. Detector performance is assessed across evaluation splits, aggregation granularities, and minimum-history settings using precision, recall, F1 score, specificity, and geometric mean. The results show that the standard z-score and Isolation Forest provide the strongest candidates among the single-layer statistical and unsupervised methods, while more complex forest variants do not justify broader tuning under the examined constraints. The final layered evaluation indicates that combining sanity checks, a z-score layer, and Isolation Forest improves recall stability across anomaly cases and operating settings. The thesis concludes that a layered detector architecture provides a practical approach for anomaly detection in competitor-pricing pipelines.

Author: Mushtaq, Muhammad Owais
Title: AI-Augmented Agile MVP Development for Lean Tech Startups
Abstract Note: Lean tech startups face many challenges to timely deliver Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) despite working in an agile environment and applying lean principles. This delayed delivery can cause product failure in terms of poor product quality or the delayed delivery itself, and sometimes even venture closure too (because some startups completely rely on one product). Most of the time, the reason behind this problem is a tight budget and a small, inefficient engineering team with scarce resources. Using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, this research included and evaluated semi-structured interviews with 18 industry practitioners to understand the problem and then proposed an AI-augmented agile MVP development framework. As per the framework, AI-assisted workflows were applied to a live enterprise setup during a legacy API migration project in two phases: inception and planning, followed by implementation and quality assurance. During the first phase, the framework reduced user story estimation time by 50% while maintaining a 94% accuracy rate compared to domain experts. In the second phase, AI-assisted development achieved up to 97% migration accuracy with minimal iteration, while AI-supported code reviews and testing improved software quality and streamlined quality assurance activities. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that AI’s effective integration can overcome the challenges of small, inefficient engineering teams. The proposed framework will help lean tech startups adopt a workable way to adopt AI-first agile workflows that increase development speed without compromising quality.

Author: de Almeida Junior, Aylton Bernardino
Title: On the use of large language models for software library migration
Abstract Note: A manutenção de software e a atualização de dependências evitam a obsolescência de sistemas. Quando bibliotecas introduzem breaking changes, desenvolvedores enfrentam refatorações custosas e propensas a erros. Em linguagens dinâmicas como Python, ferramentas tradicionais baseadas em Árvores de Sintaxe Abstrata (AST) falham devido à flexibilidade da linguagem em tempo de execução. Nesse cenário, os Large Language Models (LLMs) surgem como uma alternativa promissora, mas sua eficácia em migrações complexas demanda validação empírica. Nesta dissertação, investigamos o uso de LLMs na migração de bibliotecas em Python, utilizando as transições para a versão 2 do SQLAlchemy e Pydantic como objeto de estudo. Introduzimos a métrica de Migration Coverage para quantificar a proporção de código legado efetivamente transformado e utilizamos a porcentagem de testes que passam para avaliar o funcionamento da aplicação após a migração. A pesquisa avaliou duas abordagens: uma estática (baseada em Prompts) e uma autônoma (GitHub Copilot Agent Mode). O primeiro estudo revelou que a abordagem orientada por prompts (Zero-Shot, One-Shot e Chain-of-Thoughts) atingiu altas taxas de Migration Coverage. Contudo, apresentou pouco percentual de testes passando. Em contrapartida, o segundo estudo demonstrou que o uso do modo Agente muda esse cenário. Ao interagir com o ambiente, executar testes e analisar erros, o agente manteve alta Migration Coverage (medianas de 100% e 60% para cada biblioteca) e manteve o funcionamento. No SQLAlchemy, a mediana de testes foi de quase 40%, com 5 repositórios alcançando uma migração quase perfeita (100% de cobertura e mais de 80% de

Author: Otwell, Christopher E.
Title: DevSecOps: Design Science Research of the DevSecOps Technology Stack, Definitions, Concepts, and Improvements Identified Thereof
Abstract Note: DevSecOps is an innovative set of concepts for improving the end-state of deployed mission software with improved backed-in Cybersecurity. DevSecOps implements automated testing, cybersecurity quality scanning, source code analysis tools, immutable system design, and rapid deployment processes. The DevSecOps technology stack (s) definition and contents are immature and filled with gaps. When implemented, Agile technologies decrease system development and engineering time. DevOps processes rapidly decrease the time from initial code to mission system operations through improved software quality. DevOps focuses on software pipeline construction via automated deployments, decreasing the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)(years-to-months-to-days-to-hours) but failed to provide cybersecurity protections correctly. DevSecOps bridges the shortcomings in DevOps via additional Cybersecurity activities early within software pipeline construction. Design Science Research (DSR) into the DevSecOps reference frameworks and technology stacks was needed to improve understanding of DevSecOps. Existing frameworks and cornerstone literature reviews, coupled with DSR, improved the body of knowledge (BoK). The result was an improved and successful DevSecOps Reference Framework for implementation.

Author: Bappon, Suborno Deb
Title: Enhancing Knowledge Quality in Crowd-Sourced Developer Q&A Platforms through AI-driven Software Solutions
Abstract Note: Programming question-and-answer (Q&A) platforms have transformed how developers seek and share programming knowledge, addressing limitations of traditional documentation and tutorial resources. Among them, Stack Overflow (SO) stands as the most prominent community-driven repository where developers exchange solutions and insights. Despite its impact, SO faces persistent challenges that threaten the clarity, reliability, and longevity of its content. Many code snippets shared in answers lack inline comments, accepted answers can become outdated as technologies evolve, and subtle forms of technical debt (TD) often appear in optimization questions without explicit recognition. This thesis presents three interrelated studies that leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance the comprehensibility, adaptability, and quality awareness of knowledge shared on SO. In our first study, we focus on improving the interpretability of code snippets in SO answers. We observe that a large number of shared code examples lack meaningful inline comments, reducing their reusability, particularly for novice programmers. To address this, we develop AUTOGENICS, a context-aware tool powered by LLMs that automatically generates inline comments aligned with both the code and its corresponding question context. Through manual evaluation and practitioner feedback, AUTOGENICS demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, adequacy, conciseness, and usefulness, offering developers clearer, noise-free code explanations that enhance comprehension. While addressing code comprehensibility, we notice that even well-explained answers may lose relevance over time as technologies change. The valuable discussions embedded in user comments often remain underutilized, despite containing suggestions and corrections that could improve answer quality. Motivated by these observations, our second study introduces AUTOCOMBAT, a tool that automatically synthesizes improvement-oriented comments to produce enhanced answers. Using the ReSOlve benchmark and multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, AUTOCOMBAT integrates comment-based feedback into semantically faithful answer revisions. Evaluations using syntactic and semantic similarity metrics, along with a user survey, confirm that AUTOCOMBAT effectively transforms community feedback into coherent and updated answers while preserving technical intent, thereby promoting the continuous evolution of SO knowledge. During the investigation of answer evolution, we discover that many optimization-related questions contain signs of unacknowledged quality concerns in the form of TD, such as inefficient design or premature optimization decisions. Recognizing this gap, our third study introduces DebtNetX, a multimodal late-fusion transformer that combines textual and code representations to detect TD in SO questions. By integrating DeBERTa for text encoding and CodeBERT for code encoding, DebtNetX outperforms text-only baselines, revealing that nearly one-third of optimization-related questions on SO show latent TD. A lightweight browser plugin operationalizes this approach by enabling developers to identify the presence and type of TD, as well as reflect on potential debt indicators while engaging with community content. Collectively, these studies present complementary AI-assisted approaches for improving the clarity, currency, and quality awareness of developer knowledge on SO. Together, they contribute toward a more comprehensible, adaptive, and sustainable ecosystem of community-driven software knowledge.
