Author: Cheenepalli, Jayaprakash Reddy
Title: Evaluating and Proposing the Best Practices for DevSecOps: A Research-Based Analysis
Abstract Note: This research evaluates the adoption of DevSecOps among small to medium sized enterprises (SMEs), identifying key challenges, best practices, and future trends. Through a mixed methods approach backed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory, we analyzed survey data from 405 SME professionals, revealing that while 68% have implemented DevSecOps, adoption is hindered by technical complexity (41%), resource constraints (35%), and cultural resistance (38%). Despite strong leadership prioritization of security (73%), automation gaps persist, with only 12% of organizations performing security scans per commit.

Author: Amin, H. M.
Title: Exploring Code Version Migration Challenges Through the Lens of Neural Analysis
Abstract Note: The evolution of programming languages introduces continuous improvements in performance, maintainability, and security. However, this evolution often leads to challenges in version migration, where compatibility issues, syntax changes, and dependency management complexities become significant obstacles. Python, a widely-used language in fields like web development, data science, and machine learning, has seen considerable migration challenges, particularly during the transition from Python 2. x to Python 3. x. Despite the availability of documentation and tools, developers continue to face difficulties due to a lack of systematically categorized resources and real-world insights into migration issues. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of Python version migration challenges that consists of 1.9 million Python-related Stack Overflow (SO) posts. In this thesis, We have leveraged a multi-step process, starting with topic modeling to find the seven distinct categories and then through manual analysis of 400 random questions to build a version-migration catalogue. We expanded the manually labeled dataset to 6,905 entries through prompt-engineering the Large Language Models (LLMs) that eventually be used to build classifier to complement the catalogue. Additionally, we proposed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based tool that utilizes a vector database of Stack Overflow Q\&A pairs to assist developers by providing context-aware solutions for migration-related questions. Our contributions in this thesis are three-folds. First, we propose a novel version-migration issue related catalogue using topic modeling and manual analysis. Second, we show that leveraging few-shot prompting with human-evaluation can lead to build models to scale the dataset size further minimizing manual efforts including human-hours. Third, we provide a context-aware domain-specific consistent classifier and a RAG-Based tool that can be used for different domain-specific tasks such as automatic tagging support and provide more relevant answers to domain-specific questions. Our evaluation shows that fine-tuned DeBERTa-based classifiers achieved state-of-the-art performance in this domain with a F1-score of 77\%. Moreover, our findings revealed that library and framework compatibility issues were the most prevalent, with unanswered rates of 22.4\% and 21.8\%, and average resolution delays of 55 and 44 days, respectively. This study provides the first comprehensive exploration of Python version migration challenges by offering a fine-grained dataset, a deeper understanding of migration-related challenges, and foundational work towards practical, scalable automated migration assistance tools.

Author: Sharma, Vikas; Kar, Arpan K.
Title: From Agentic AI to Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Framework for Responsible AI
Abstract Note: Autonomous AI systems, termed" agentic AI," demonstrate remarkable capabilities in pursuing complex objectives with minimal human oversight yet introduce critical challenges: output hallucinations, opaque decision making, and governance fragility. This conceptual paper examines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) as a strategic architectural pivot embedding traceability directly into generative processes. The discussion contextualizes how agentic autonomy amplifies both innovation potential and systemic risk within sociotechnical ecosystems, emphasizing the importance of embedding auditability and interpretability as intrinsic design features, than retrospective controls. It illustrates how RAG driven architectures can reconcile operational efficiency with regulatory compliance through adaptive evidence generation and contextual reasoning. By synthesizing academic literature with industry frameworks, this research proposes actionable pathways for organizations transitioning towards accountable AI systems. This analysis, grounded in the Bright Origin Perspective, contributes a unified framework positioning RAG not as a technical enhancement but as an ethical imperative for sustainable digital transformation, culminating in responsible AI

Author: Zhao, Gengwu
Title: Detecting and Refactoring Mock Clones in Java Test Code: From Empirical Evidence to Automated Framework
Abstract Note: Mocking frameworks such as Mockito, EasyMock, and PowerMock are widely used in modern unit testing to isolate dependencies and improve test controllability. However, their adoption introduces a distinct form of redundancy that differs from traditional code clones. Unlike contiguous and syntactically similar clones, mock-related duplication consists of fine-grained, semantically similar API sequences for mock creation, stubbing, and verification that are scattered across test cases and interleaved with unrelated logic. These characteristics make mock clones largely invisible to existing clone detection tools.

Author: Aljemabi, Mohammed Abdelrahman; Ali, Mohammed Babiker; Mohammed, Mohammed Eltayb
Title: An Empirical Study on Developer Migration and Sentiment: Framework Evolution vs. Backward Compatibility
Abstract Note: The stability of software frameworks is a fundamental pillar of project sustainability. This paper investigates the phenomenon of” breaking changes” and their association on developer migration, utilizing transitions in major ecosystems—primarily AngularJS to Angular/React, expanded to include Vue. js and Svelte—as a comprehensive case study. Moving beyond traditional cross platform studies, our methodology leverages a unified data source approach by mining both technical artifacts (commit logs) and Developer Social Networks (DSN) interactions (Issues and Pull Request discussions) exclusively within the GitHub ecosystem. By employing API diffing algorithms and a domain-specific BERT model for Natural Language Processing (NLP) sentiment analysis (Accuracy: 89%), we analyzed a dataset of 5,240 commits and 2,150 explicit migration events. Our findings demonstrate that the lack of backward compatibility generated profound cognitive fatigue and negative sentiment (Average Sentiment:-0.62). Statistical modeling, including Pearson correlation (r=-0.74, p¡ 0.01) and logistic regression, reveals a statistically significant association between breaking changes, developer sentiment, and migration behavior. This frustration directly correlated with a structural exodus toward alternative frameworks, heavily favoring incremental strategies like React Adapters and Micro Frontends over complete rewrites to escape the ecosystem’s instability. The study highlights how a lack of backward compatibility inflicts severe socio-technical debt, driving developers to abandon frameworks altogether.

Author: Esberger, Manuel
Title: Designing Cloud Applications for Compatibility: A Case Study on Kubernetes and OpenShift
Abstract Note: The transition from monolithic architectures to microservices has established Kubernetes a viable solution for container orchestration, yet the ecosystem remains fragmented across diverse implementations like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and OpenShift. This fragmentation introduces compatibility challenges for DevOps teams, primarily due to vendor-specific configurations and API evolutions. This thesis investigates these challenges through a Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) and a Multivocal Literature Review, identifying API deprecations, networking, and deployment tooling as the areas of friction in the practitioner community.Central to this research is a case study involving the migration of the DBRepo application from an AKS environment to a more restrictive private OpenShift cluster. Through this "lift-and-shift" process, we formulated several design patterns to enhance application portability. A primary finding is that designing for the most restrictive security environments—specifically complying with OpenShift’s restricted-v2 Security Context Constraints (SCC) inherently improves compatibility across less stringent platforms.Furthermore, we propose a platform-independent gateway service to abstract away vendor-specific Ingress and Route configurations, facilitating a single codebase for multiple cluster types.The proposed design patterns were validated on a Minikube instance, serving as a baseline for vendor-agnosticism. The evaluation demonstrated that 6 out of 9 compatibility categories functioned "out of the box" without reconfiguration. While manual efforts remained necessary for storage onboarding and dependency updates, the results indicate that prioritizing minimal privilege requirements and architectural abstraction reduces the technical debt and effort associated with cross-platform cloud migrations.

Author: Sveinbjarnarson, Bjarki Freyr
Title: Scaling Data Governance Through Automation and Dynamic Data Spaces
Abstract Note:
Managing vast amounts of heterogeneous data is a growing challenge in healthcare research, where data must be structured, stored, and validated for diverse research purposes while minimizing the manual resources required for maintenance. This thesis explores scalable data management solutions, focusing on database design, data quality enforcement, and automated data governance to ensure usability across research disciplines. We designed and developed a homogeneous database structure capable of accommodating a wide range of structured health data while minimizing complexity and ensuring flexibility for future research needs. This database architecture enables the seamless integration of new data sources without expanding storage requirements, making it a scalable solution for large-scale research projects. Additionally, we implemented a validation system embedded within a digital infrastructure to enforce predefined data standards, reducing errors at the point of entry and improving data quality.
The empirical work underlying this thesis is based on four studies conducted within a large sleep research project encompassing diverse datasets. First, we evaluated the feasibility of displaying key dataset insights through a digital infrastructure, providing researchers with an overview of stored data. Second, we developed a homogeneous database framework that eliminates the need for additional tables as new data sources are added. Third, we conducted a study to identify the root causes of poor data quality at the input stage, analyzing how researchers interact with data validation mechanisms and where errors emerge. Lastly, we examined data governance models that minimize human intervention while maintaining research integrity, ensuring sustainability in data management. Findings from these studies reveal common causes of poor data

Author: Sylla, Mai
Title: Architectural Strategies for Building Resilient Software Infrastructure in Rapidly Evolving Digital Environments
Abstract Note:
The contemporary digital environment is characterized by accelerating technological change, volatile operational demands, and an ever-expanding threat landscape, conditions that place unprecedented pressure on the architectural foundations of software infrastructure. Resilient software infrastructure must not merely withstand disruption but adapt, recover, and continue delivering value under conditions of uncertainty. This abstract synthesizes a broad body of foundational and contemporary scholarship to articulate architectural strategies that enable such resilience. Central to this inquiry is the recognition that resilience is not a single property but an emergent outcome of interdependent design decisions spanning modularity, abstraction, fault tolerance, security, and continuous evolution. The architectural principles embedded in deep compositional models, attention-based sequence transduction, residual learning, and generative adversarial frameworks offer instructive analogies for software systems that must learn, adapt, and self-correct in real time. These computational paradigms demonstrate that layered abstraction, skip connections, and adversarial validation can stabilize learning and performance under noisy or shifting conditions, principles that translate directly into architectural tactics such as graceful degradation, redundancy, and continuous integration of feedback signals.
The challenge of technical debt represents a critical dimension of infrastructure resilience, as accumulated shortcuts and deferred maintenance erode the capacity of systems to absorb change. Quantifying technical debt and understanding its impact on delivery performance enables organizations to make informed trade-offs between shortterm velocity and long-term adaptability. Architectural strategies that institutionalize debt visibility, refactoring cadences, and modular boundaries help prevent the silent accumulation of fragility. In parallel, the security posture of software infrastructure must be treated as an architectural concern rather than a peripheral compliance activity. The integration of cryptographic verification, distributed ledger mechanisms, and zero-trust principles into the fabric of system design provides tamper-evident auditability and strengthens resistance to adversarial compromise. Security architectures that embed blockchain-inspired immutability and decentralized validation into critical pathways offer promising avenues for protecting integrity in environments where centralized trust models are increasingly untenable.

Author: May, Elliot; Walters, Leo; Mahra, Natin; Jimenez, Bjorn
Title: Customer Experience Intelligence Through Aspect-Level Sentiment Analysis of Online Reviews
Abstract Note: Aspect-level sentiment analysis has become a central analytical instrument for transforming unstructured online reviews into structured evidence about customer experience. Unlike document-level sentiment classification, aspect-level approaches attempt to link evaluative language to discrete product attributes, service components, and interaction properties, thereby producing a multidimensional view of customer satisfaction and dissatisfaction. This paper presents a system-oriented examination of customer experience intelligence based on aspect-level sentiment analysis. It analyzes architectural choices that connect review ingestion, aspect extraction, sentiment classification, aggregation, and managerial reporting. Emphasis is placed on structural trade-offs between modular pipelines and end-to-end learning, the governance of training data and model outputs, and the operational requirements for stable deployment in consumer-facing platforms. The discussion further addresses robustness under linguistic variation, fairness across user groups and product categories, transparency in automated decision support, and sustainability of large-scale natural language processing infrastructure. By situating technical advances within broader socio-technical systems, the paper argues that aspect-level sentiment intelligence should be designed as a governed, continuous, interpretable, and accountable organizational capability rather than an isolated classification task. The analysis integrates conceptual foundations, cross-domain illustrations, deployment constraints, and policy implications to provide a research and practice agenda for responsible customer experience intelligence systems.

Author: Cho, Yeon
Title: Protecting Academic Information Systems Through Integrated Cybersecurity Governance and Infrastructure Management
Abstract Note:
Academic information systems have become indispensable infrastructure for research, teaching, administration, and knowledge dissemination across higher education institutions worldwide. Yet the same digital transformation that has expanded institutional capabilities has also introduced a widening array of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, ranging from ransomware and phishing to supply-chain compromises and insider threats. These vulnerabilities are no longer isolated technical problems; they are systemic governance challenges that intersect with institutional strategy, workforce development, regulatory compliance, and ethical stewardship. Addressing them effectively requires a framework that integrates cybersecurity governance with infrastructure management rather than treating the two as separate domains. This study draws on a synthesis of research in cybersecurity education, national strategy, artificial intelligence, blockchain technology, and organizational culture to propose and examine an integrated model for protecting academic information systems. The central argument is that sustainable cybersecurity in higher education depends on the alignment of policy architecture, technical infrastructure, human capacity, and institutional culture, each reinforcing the other rather than operating in isolation.
National cybersecurity strategies increasingly emphasize education and workforce development as foundational pillars, recognizing that technological controls alone cannot compensate for insufficient human expertise or weak institutional governance. Cybersecurity education initiatives, workforce frameworks, and competency models have emerged to define the knowledge, skills, and abilities required of information security professionals. Within academic institutions, these frameworks carry particular significance because universities serve dual roles: they are both targets of cyberattacks and producers of the next generation of cybersecurity talent. The integration of cybersecurity curricula with operational security practices creates a feedback loop in which students gain practical experience while institutions benefit from heightened security awareness. However, the effectiveness of such integration depends on organizational commitment, adequate resourcing, and governance structures that clearly assign accountability for information security across administrative and academic units.

Author: Bakhaev, Stepan
Title: On stakeholder dialectics in digital identity infrastructures
Abstract Note: This thesis studies change in identity management in the context of digital public service delivery. Identity management involves actors, processes and supporting technologies for the creation, management and use of digital identities—the information about individuals necessary for access to varied services. Software-based systems for identity management are undergoing a considerable change, coupled with the decentralised communication and distributed decision-making for digital identities, which gives individuals greater control over personal information. This brings organisational complexity in system development and calls for consideration of stakeholder relations when specifying system requirements, managing interests and making architectural decisions that influence the scope of change in the digital infrastructures of public services. The goal of this thesis is to analyse stakeholder relations during system development. The analysis is based on a series of qualitative field studies within a large inter-organisational project in Europe. The project focused on the development of an electronic identification system for online public services and involved software developers, citizens and public administrations in a collaborative design process. The research combined observational and participatory components from the empirical setting and proceeded in three phases. First, the study explored requirements for the system design using co-creation principles. Second, the study investigated architectural assumptions underpinning design decisions during the system development. Third, the study conducted a comprehensive stakeholder analysis to examine the role of symbolic properties and trust in the system adoption. The results emphasise the need to shift attention in identity management decentralisation from technical designs to the social and organisational factors that influence design during system development. The integration of user-centred identity management systems into the digital infrastructures of public services requires engaging stakeholders in a dialogic exploration of their infrastructural relations. By supporting institutional transparency and inclusivity in the design of digital identity technology, practitioners and policymakers can promote trust in emergent decentralised solutions. Thus, this thesis aims to contribute to knowledge of identity management for public services as socio-technical systems shaped by stakeholders’ infrastructural relations.

Author: Bae, Matteo
Title: The Impact of Distributed System Architecture on IT Infrastructure Performance During Organizational Growth
Abstract Note:
Organizational growth imposes escalating and often contradictory demands on information technology infrastructure, transforming what begins as a modest, coherent technical environment into a heterogeneous assemblage of servers, services, data stores, and communication pathways whose collective behavior becomes progressively harder to predict, govern, and sustain. Distributed system architecture has emerged as the dominant response to this pressure, promising horizontal extensibility, fault isolation, and the elastic allocation of computational resources across many cooperating nodes. Yet the relationship between distributed design and realized infrastructure performance during periods of rapid organizational expansion is neither linear nor uniformly beneficial. This abstract synthesizes a wide body of scholarly work spanning digital strategy, organizational capability, software architecture evaluation, edge and cloud computing, energy systems, and resilience theory to articulate a nuanced account of how distribution shapes performance outcomes as enterprises scale.
A central tension animating the literature concerns the migration from monolithic to decentralized architectures. Comparative performance and scalability evaluations consistently indicate that microservice-based and otherwise distributed designs can deliver superior throughput and fault tolerance under growing load, but these gains are contingent on sophisticated orchestration, observability, and operational discipline. Distributed architectures convert many formerly internal failure modes into network-mediated ones, introducing latency, partial failure, consistency challenges, and cascading dependency risks that monoliths largely avoid. Consequently, the performance benefits of distribution are realized only when organizations simultaneously invest in the sociotechnical capabilities required to manage complexity, a theme echoed in historical analyses of industrial enterprise capabilities and in contemporary treatments of organizational resilience. Infrastructure performance during growth is therefore best understood not as a purely technical property but as an emergent outcome of architectural choices interacting with organizational learning, governance, and adaptive capacity.

Author: Kobayashi, Suresh
Title: Investigating the Operational Consequences of Legacy Software Components on Enterprise Security and System Reliability
Abstract Note: The operational consequences of legacy software components within enterprise environments constitute a systemic risk that simultaneously degrades security posture and undermines system reliability, producing cascading failures that transcend traditional boundaries between cybersecurity and operational resilience. Legacy components, defined as software artifacts whose support lifecycles have expired, whose architectural assumptions predate contemporary threat models, or whose integration interfaces resist modernization, remain embedded within critical infrastructure across sectors including finance, healthcare, energy, and transportation. Their persistence is rarely accidental; rather, it reflects rational short-term economic decisions, institutional inertia, and the substantial technical debt accumulated through decades of incremental modification. The interaction between these components and modern security mechanisms creates a paradox: the very systems designed to protect enterprise assets frequently cannot be applied to legacy subsystems without risking operational disruption, forcing organizations into a precarious equilibrium where security controls are selectively relaxed to preserve availability. This equilibrium is inherently unstable. Legacy components often operate with elevated privileges, rely on deprecated cryptographic primitives, and expose unauthenticated interfaces that were acceptable within perimeter-defended network architectures but become critical vulnerabilities within zero-trust paradigms. The reliability consequences are equally severe. Legacy software frequently exhibits undocumented behavioral dependencies, hardcoded configuration assumptions, and resource management practices incompatible with containerized or elastic deployment models. When such components fail under load, the failure modes are often non-graceful, producing data corruption, silent transaction loss, or cascading timeouts that propagate through service meshes and API gateways. The operational burden of maintaining these components diverts engineering capacity from strategic initiatives, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which technical debt compounds while the organization's ability to remediate it diminishes. Quantitative assessments of technical debt consistently demonstrate that legacy components impose disproportionate costs relative to their functional contribution, yet removal or replacement efforts are frequently deferred due to perceived migration risks and the absence of comprehensive dependency mapping. From a security operations perspective, legacy components generate log formats incompatible with modern SIEM platforms, lack support for structured threat intelligence feeds, and cannot participate in automated incident response workflows. This visibility gap means that intrusions pivoting through legacy subsystems may remain undetected for extended periods, while forensic reconstruction is hampered by incomplete or inconsistently retained audit trails. The reliability engineering community has long recognized that complex systems fail in complex ways, and legacy components introduce failure modes that are neither fully understood nor adequately tested. Their presence complicates capacity planning, disaster recovery validation, and fault isolation exercises. Furthermore, regulatory frameworks increasingly mandate software bill of materials transparency, vulnerability disclosure timelines, and patch management cadences that legacy components cannot satisfy without extensive compensating controls. The convergence of security and reliability concerns is particularly acute in operational technology environments

Author: Hirani, Sandeep
Title: LLMigrate: An LLM-Based System for Legacy ML Code Migration
Abstract Note:
Machine learning research often relies on foundational papers whose code was written using older library versions. While these papers remain highly influential, reproducing results in modern environments poses significant challenges. Core APIs have been deprecated, execution paradigms have shifted, and migration often requires deep expertise across framework versions.

This creative component presents an automated migration system that leverages large language models (LLMs) to modernize legacy machine learning repositories. The system combines RAG-based retrieval using a FAISS vector index and sentence-transformer embeddings over a curated migration knowledge base, with multi-layer validation including syntax, compilation, import resolution, framework-specific heuristics, and optional runtime execution. It also incorporates iterative error-feedback refinement with up to five retry attempts.

Dependency-aware processing using AST parsing and topological sorting ensures inter-file compatibility, while contextual prompts preserve cross-file interfaces. The system has been evaluated primarily on TensorFlow and PyTorch, with additional support for NumPy, JAX, scikit-learn, and Keras. Results demonstrate significant improvements in migration speed, correctness, and completeness compared to manual and rule-based approaches.

Author: Kollari, Sai Sree Harsha
Title: Self-evolving Software Reliability Intelligence: A Continual Learning and Uncertainty-aware Framework for Cross-project Defect Prediction, Adaptive Risk Governance, and Autonomous Quality Assurance
Abstract Note: Software defect prediction is commonly formulated as a stationary supervised-learning problem, although production software evolves through releases, architectural changes, dependency updates, shifting development practices, and heterogeneous project contexts. These changes can invalidate a model after deployment and can make point predictions appear more certain than the available evidence warrants. This paper proposes Self-Evolving Software Reliability Intelligence (SRI), a framework that unifies cross-project defect prediction, continual adaptation, predictive uncertainty, drift-aware model governance, and quality-assurance decision policies. SRI separates representation transfer from temporal adaptation and places an uncertainty-aware decision layer between prediction and engineering action. The framework maintains a bounded replay memory, monitors distributional and performance drift, calibrates predictive confidence, and selects among model reuse, incremental update, and controlled retraining. A risk-governance policy combines defect probability, uncertainty, software criticality, and inspection cost to prioritize testing without treating machine-learning output as an autonomous release authority. Because no original experimental measurements were supplied for this manuscript, the paper deliberately reports no fabricated accuracy, AUC, cost reduction, or statistical significance. Instead, it defines a reproducible evaluation protocol, hypotheses, ablations, metrics, and acceptance criteria that can be executed on public multi-project, multi-version defect datasets. The resulting contribution is a technically specified research framework and empirical design for studying whether adaptive, uncertainty-aware reliability intelligence can remain useful under cross-project distribution shift and software evolution.

Author: Re, Francesco
Title: Integration of Intelligent agents in Game Development: Prompt Engineering Methodologies for Automatic code generation
Abstract Note: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within software engineering has significantly expanded following the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and natural language processing. These technologies have been implemented across a vast array of techniques to optimize developer workflows, a trend that is equally prominent in game development. While current research predominantly focuses on generating complete, end-to-end experiences via prompts and agentic architectures, this study explores the use of LLMs as tools to enhance a developer's architectural design, effectively translating creative intent into technical implementation. Utilizing prompt engineering techniques, this research aims to develop a short game project featuring exploration and a turn-based combat system. The project was built using the Unity engine, with most game object components generated entirely through AI code generation. The methodology relied on two main approaches: detailed file specifications and a multi-level prompting strategy that progressively narrowed the scope toward full class implementation. Once the initial classes were generated, a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approach was adopted to integrate additional mechanics and resolve anomalies. To execute this framework, local models were utilized, specifically Qwen3-coder 30B. The empirical results indicate that across 149 prompts used to create 24 classes, these strategies generated code that rarely exhibited syntax errors, aligned consistently with the initial design, and largely avoided hallucinating divergent functions. Each class required an average of 12 prompts (with a median value of 4). The majority of the prompts (96) were used within the HITL phase to refine results, while the remaining 53 prompts were dedicated to class building and implementing new features. However, this methodology revealed constraints in specific areas. Hallucinations were not entirely eliminated, averaging 0.88 per class (with a median of 0). Furthermore, longer implementations degraded model efficiency, occasionally leading to corrupted outputs. Finally, the strict constraints of the prompting framework made the final implementation heavily dependent on the initial design, leaving the model with little autonomy to correct foundational flaws in the architecture. Overall, this study demonstrates that the proposed framework enables the creation of game projects with minimal programming language expertise, shifting the developer's core requirement toward critical thinking and design validation.

Author: Rayarao, Surya Rao; Donikena, Naga
Title: Design Trade-offs in REST API Data Transfer Object Architecture: Centralized vs. Independent DTO Patterns in Enterprise Software Development
Abstract Note: Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) serve as a fundamental architectural pattern in REST API development, facilitating data exchange between client and server while maintaining separation of concerns. This paper examines the critical design decision between implementing centralized shared DTOs versus independent API-specific DTOs in enterprise software systems. Through comprehensive analysis of both approaches, we evaluate the implications for code maintainability, system flexibility, and long-term evolution in the context of modern software quality metrics, particularly those enforced by static analysis tools like SonarQube. Our investigation reveals that while centralized DTOs offer immediate benefits in code reuse and reduced duplication, independent DTOs provide superior adaptability for evolving business requirements. We present detailed examples, analyze real-world scenarios, and provide guidelines for architects and developers making these crucial design decisions. The findings suggest that the optimal choice depends heavily on project maturity, expected evolution patterns, and organizational priorities regarding maintainability versus flexibility.

Author: Patel, Tejendra
Title: Migrating Enforcement Infrastructure from Legacy Systems to Modern Compute Engines: A Comprehensive Study of Large-Scale Anti-Scraping Platform Evolution
Abstract Note: The evolution of enforcement infrastructure from legacy compute engines to modern platforms represents a critical challenge in contemporary software engineering environments. The migration of Meta's anti-scraping enforcement platform from the Haskell-based Sigma compute engine to the Omega platform exemplifies the complexities inherent in large-scale infrastructure modernization initiatives. The transition encompasses extensive feature sets and multiple policy endpoints while maintaining zero service degradation and enforcement accuracy throughout the migration process. The methodology employs systematic dependency discovery, comprehensive feature parity verification, and advanced regression validation frameworks to ensure seamless platform evolution. Proactive observability mechanisms and staged rollout strategies guarantee system reliability across high-volume production environments processing billions of daily transactions. Advanced dependency analysis tools enable identification of hidden system interconnections while automated testing frameworks validate functional equivalence between legacy and modern implementations. Performance optimization techniques demonstrate substantial improvements in system scalability and operational efficiency following migration completion. The comprehensive validation framework successfully preserves institutional knowledge while enabling future platform enhancement capabilities. The successful implementation establishes effective practices for de-risking infrastructure evolution while maintaining enforcement efficacy in mission-critical production environments.

Author: Orazov, Y.; Kulov, N.; Yarashova, G.
Title: THE ARCHITECTURAL SYNERGY: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND CLOUD COMPUTING
Abstract Note: This article examines the evolving partnership between traditional Software Engineering and Cloud Computing, moving beyond local development to a globally distributed, scalable architecture. It explores three critical pillars: the transition from monolithic to microservices architecture, the implementation of DevOps and Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and the financial and operational shift toward serverless computing. The text highlights that while Software Engineering focuses on the logic and quality of code, Cloud Computing provides the elastic infrastructure necessary to handle modern data loads and global accessibility. Ultimately, the article argues for an integrated "Cloud-Native" model where software reliability and infrastructure agility are treated as mutually reinforcing objectives. In the modern technological landscape, the silos between code development and server management are disappearing. The synergy between Software Engineering and Cloud Computing is no longer just a technical convenience; it is the engine that drives digital transformation. While Software Engineering focuses on the "logic" side—algorithms, data structures, and user experience—Cloud Computing provides the data-driven framework to ensure those applications are scalable, resilient, and cost-effective.

Author: Syed, Allamuddin; Maher, Syeda Salma; Weber, Mark; Basavaraju, Srinidhi
Title: A Codec-Infrastructure Framework for the OTT Era Artificial Intelligence• Codec Architecture• OTT Infrastructure Economics
Abstract Note: The global Pay TV market has shed over 25% of its subscriber base since 2017, and OTT delivery has become the dominant medium for video consumption worldwide. This structural shift has transformed encoding infrastructure from a back-office cost centre into a first-order competitive variable—one where the wrong decision translates directly into tens of millions of dollars in avoidable CDN expenditure, degraded viewer experience, and technical debt that compounds with every hour of content ever encoded.

Author: Nidheesh Sharma, Dr Neha Gupta
Title: Integrating Traditional Risk Management Practices with Agile Software Development: A Hybrid Framework for Improved Risk Handling
Abstract Note: Software projects continue to overrun schedule and budget for reasons that disciplined risk management was designed to prevent. Plan-driven risk management, as codified in PMBOK, PRINCE2 and ISO 31000, offers rigorous identification, quantification and traceability, but its heavyweight documentation cycles fit poorly with short iterations and emergent requirements. Agile methods handle volatility well through short feedback loops, yet they treat risk implicitly, rarely quantify exposure, and consistently underperform on slow-moving systemic risks such as architectural erosion, vendor dependency and regulatory compliance. This paper proposes HARM-F (Hybrid Agile Risk Management Framework), a two-tier framework that retains a lightweight strategic risk register and quantitative exposure model from traditional practice while embedding risk activities directly in agile ceremonies at the tactical tier. The framework introduces a composite Hybrid Risk Score that combines probability, impact, volatility and detectability with analytic-hierarchy-process weights, a risk-velocity measure that converts the static register into an iteration-level trend signal, and a benefit-ratio rule for selecting responses. HARM-F was developed through a design-science cycle informed by a practitioner survey and evaluated on six industrial projects against matched control projects. The treatment group showed a 37.9 percent gain in risk-detection effectiveness, a 60.8 percent reduction in escaped risks, and schedule and cost variance reduced to 7.4 and 6.8 percent respectively, at an additional process overhead of roughly four percent of iteration effort.

Author: Sánchez, Rafał
Title: Economic Evaluation of Tiered Solution Architecture for Strategic Planning and Execution of Large-Scale Digital Transformation Projects
Abstract Note: This study presents an economic evaluation framework for tiered solution architecture as a strategic approach to planning and executing large-scale digital transformation initiatives. The research addresses a critical gap in the literature: while digital transformation is widely recognized as essential for organizational competitiveness, the economic justification for specific architectural choices—particularly the adoption of tiered structures—remains underexplored. The proposed framework synthesizes principles from software architecture, strategic management, and cost-benefit analysis to model the financial implications of deploying a layered system comprising presentation, business logic, data, and integration tiers. The evaluation employs a mixed-methods design, combining quantitative simulation of total cost of ownership (TCO), return on investment (ROI), and net present value (NPV) with qualitative case study analysis of three multinational corporations that have undertaken multi-year digital transformation programs. The quantitative component simulates a typical large-scale transformation scenario involving 15,000 users, 200 microservices, and a five-year implementation horizon. Results indicate that organizations adopting a tiered architecture achieve a 28% reduction in long-term maintenance costs compared to monolithic alternatives, primarily due to modular component reuse and independent scalability. The tiered approach also demonstrates a 22% improvement in deployment frequency and a 35% reduction in mean time to recovery, translating into measurable productivity gains. The qualitative findings reveal that tiered architectures facilitate strategic alignment by enabling incremental investment: organizations can prioritize high-impact tiers—such as customer-facing presentation layers—while deferring less critical backend components, thereby reducing upfront capital expenditure by an average of 18%. However, the analysis also identifies significant upfront costs associated with tiered architecture implementation, including a 15% premium in initial development expenses due to the need for interface contracts, orchestration logic, and cross-tier testing. The economic break-even point typically occurs in the third year of operation. The study further introduces a risk-adjusted economic model that accounts for technology obsolescence, vendor lock-in, and organizational resistance to change. The model demonstrates that tiered architectures offer superior risk mitigation through encapsulation: changes to one tier rarely cascade across others, reducing the probability of costly systemic failures by 40%. Sensitivity analysis reveals that the economic viability of tiered architecture is most sensitive to two variables: the cost of integration testing and the expected lifespan of the technology stack. When these factors are unfavorable, the tiered approach may underperform simpler architectures. The research concludes with a decision-support tool that enables executives to evaluate tiered architecture against alternative patterns—including event-driven and service-oriented architectures—based on organization-specific parameters such as team size, regulatory complexity, and existing technical debt. The tool recommends tiered architecture for organizations with high long-term strategic ambiguity, as the modular structure preserves options for future pivots. Theoretical contributions include extending transaction cost economics to the domain of digital architecture, demonstrating that tiered structures reduce coordination costs across specialized teams while increasing the specificity of investments.

Author: Han, Yushi
Title: MLOps and LLMOps engineering for deployment and evaluation of AI models
Abstract Note: This Master thesis presents the work conducted during my internship at SAP France within the CPIT-Big Data & Machine Learning Foundation team, focusing on MLOps and LLMOps engineering. The project was divided into two main tasks. The first task aimed at deploying machine learning models on two different serving platforms, Azure Databricks and SAP AI Core, with a detailed analysis of performance metrics, operational reliability, and deployment workflows. The results were summarized in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) to guide future deployment decisions. The second task addressed the evaluation of Generative AI applications by designing a proof-of-concept evaluation pipeline using the “LLM-as-a-judge” methodology. Built on Databricks and orchestrated with MLflow 3. x, the pipeline enabled automated scoring of large language model outputs against criteria such as correctness, relevance, and cultural adaptation. The solution demonstrated how standardized, reusable evaluation workflows can be integrated into CI/CD environments to ensure traceability, scalability, and reproducibility. Through these tasks, this thesis highlights both the technical and methodological contributions of combining MLOps and LLMOps practices. The experience provided valuable insights into cloud-based deployment, automated evaluation of AI models, and the integration of enterprise-grade infrastructures. It confirmed the relevance of robust MLOps and LLMOps frameworks to accelerate the development, deployment, and assessment of AI systems in professional environments.

Author: Chindanuru, Rajkumar
Title: LEGACY APPLICATION MODERNIZATION IN A MANUFACTURING INDUSTRY
Abstract Note: This article examines the comprehensive modernization initiative undertaken by a clothing manufacturer to transform its production tracking and payroll processing operations. It details the challenges of legacy systems in manufacturing environments, focusing on operational inefficiencies, maintenance costs, and technical limitations that hinder business performance. It outlines a strategic modernization approach encompassing API-led integration, cloud migration, and architectural transformation.

Author: Wiedemann, Anna; Miscione, Gianluca
Title: Enabling Innovation in Digital Hospital Ecosystems-A Literature Review
Abstract Note: Healthcare information technology holds great potential for improving services in hospital environments. This transformation is fueled by the fact that current extraordinary situations, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, indicate that the realization of digital health innovation is essential to delivering most healthcare services for patients. To facilitate an environment that allows digital innovation and integration of internal and external stakeholders a movement toward a digital hospital ecosystem is needed. We conducted a structured literature review to identify the current state of knowledge about enabling mechanisms that facilitate the development of a digital hospital ecosystem. Therefore, we draw on the current literature on digital infrastructures and platform ecosystems. We identified the challenges hospitals face during their transformation and address them by deriving key mechanisms of the digital hospital ecosystem. Thus, this study contributes to research by presenting insights into the transformation toward a digital hospital ecosystem.

Author: Kolmanič, Tomaž
Title: CODORQ: ogrodje za orkestracijo razvoja programske opreme z različnimi agentskimi orodji
Abstract Note: This paper presents CODORQ, a local-first framework for orchestrating software development with various agent tools. It is based on the observation that when multiple agents work simultaneously, the limitation is not only the capacity of the models, but also the lack of a persistent, verifiable coordination layer. CODORQ connects Codex CLI, Claude Code and Antigravity CLI sessions via a local MCP server to repositories, separate Git worktrees, terminals and a common model of tasks, roles, statuses, reviews, QA results and memory. The system supports the separation of duties between execution, review and QA, tracks the identity and liveness of sessions and treats a human as the execution manager. Persistent records allow for context recovery after a crash or restart without relying on terminal rewriting. The paper describes the architecture, multi-level persistent memory, task statuses, operator web interface and defense mechanisms for restarts, unresponsive sessions, excessive MCP responses and concurrent changes. A demonstration example of the development of a small UI component shows the path from a request through a proof commit and independent review to a QA result. The paper does not demonstrate productivity gains, but rather shows how multi-agent work can be made traceable, reproducible, and operator-manageable.

Author: Badmus, Olaniyi; Jooda, Demilade; Ozowara, David Excel; Anunagba, Chukwudera Obumneke
Title: A Systematic Review of MuleSoft ESB Integration Patterns in Multi-Cloud Salesforce Architectures
Abstract Note: Enterprise organizations increasingly operate Salesforce within multi-cloud architectures that integrate diverse on-premises systems, cloud platforms, and data repositories through middleware integration layers. MuleSoft, acquired by Salesforce in 2018, has emerged as the dominant integration platform for enterprise Salesforce architectures, providing an enterprise service bus (ESB) and API-led connectivity framework that structures data exchange across complex system landscapes. Despite the prevalence of MuleSoft in enterprise Salesforce integration architectures, the academic literature lacks a systematic synthesis of the integration patterns, design principles, and architectural trade-offs that characterize MuleSoft ESB implementations in multi-cloud Salesforce contexts. This paper presents a systematic review of MuleSoft ESB integration patterns as applied in multi-cloud Salesforce architectures. The review identifies and synthesizes the principal integration patterns documented in the technical and practitioner literature, including API-led connectivity, event-driven integration, batch data exchange, real-time synchronization, and orchestration patterns. For each pattern, the review examines the architectural principles underlying pattern selection, the trade-offs between alternative implementations, and the governance requirements for maintaining integration health in production environments. The review further addresses the security, performance, and observability considerations that condition integration reliability in enterprise multicloud contexts.

Author: Islam, Syful
Title: Understanding Third-party Library Discussions Through Question-and-Answer Sites
Abstract Note:
Third-party libraries have become an integral part of modern software devel-opment, as developers have access to many useful libraries through the software packaging ecosystems. Managing third-party libraries is one of the major chal-lenges of the software ecosystem due to its high degree of interdependence. In addition, it is difficult for developers to understand the challenges and infor-mation needs of using third-party libraries from different ecosystems during the software development process. Question-and-answer sites are a popular source of knowledge for communicating developer challenges.
This thesis investigates third-party package (i.e., library) related discussions through a popular question-and-answer site such as Stack Overflow to understand the developer's experience (i.e., the challenges and information needs) of using third-party packages from different software packaging ecosystems. The main contributions of this thesis are divided into two parts. In the first part, developer's experience in package management is investigated, and found that discussion topics vary by packaging ecosystem. The results also indicate that certain features (e.g., dependency tree, environment, etc.) of package management correlate with the developer's experience. In the second part of the thesis, the investigation into package usage reveals that developers encounter different types of errors while maintaining third-party packages. Furthermore, popular packages are less likely to be discussed on Stack Overflow, indicating fewer issues relating to their usage. Finally, analyzing accepted answers shows that the answers, which include usage examples and execution commands, help resolve errors related to package usage.

Author: Ducasse, Stéphane
Title: Evref: Reflective Evolution of Ever-running Software Systems
Abstract Note: The objectives of Evref are to study and support the continuous evolution of large software systems in a holistic manner following three main axes: (1) analyses and approaches for migration and evolution of existing (legacy) systems, (2) new tools to support daily evolution, and (3) infrastructure to build language runtimes to support software evolution, new tools, frugal systems, and security language features. In the context of the first axis, Evref proposes a specific research agenda with Berger-Levrault R&D.

Author: Muse, Biruk Asmare; Khomh, Foutse; Saarimäki, Nyyti; Moreschini, Sergio; Lenarduzzi, Valentina
Title: SANER 2022
Abstract Note: Presents the table of contents/splash page of the proceedings record.

Author: Garcia, Patrick; Benites, Edson; Domingues, Ernane; Geraldo, André; Moreira de Oliveira, Flavio; Kich, Marcos; Raeder, Mateus; Sramare, André; Venkatesan, Balaji; Righi, Rodrigo da Rosa
Title: On Migrating Framework Components in Web Applications: A State-of-the-Art and State-of-the-Practice Review
Abstract Note: The evolution of web technologies requires the continuous modernization of web applications, often necessitating the migration of existing components to newer frameworks, libraries, or architectures. This survey article addresses the critical need for effective migration strategies and tools by examining the academic and practical state-of-the-art with respect to tools and frameworks. Unlike related studies, this study synthesizes findings from the most recent scholarly literature and an extensive collection of currently available tools identified through a systematic internet-based investigation. By establishing a connection between theoretical advancements and real-world implementations, this survey contributes with a comprehensive understanding of the challenges, methodologies, and tooling landscape surrounding web application component migration. In addition to architectural details, our survey stands out by providing insights on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in contemporary contexts. In addition, the article identifies emerging trends, benchmarks, best practices, and areas of potential future research and development in the critical field of software evolution. In conclusion, this integrated perspective equips researchers and practitioners with the knowledge necessary to navigate the complexities of component migration, select tools appropriately, and implement strategies for evolving web applications.

Author: Verma, Dinesh; Madni, Azad M.; Hoffenson, Steven; Xiao, Lu
Title: The Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Systems Engineering Research
Abstract Note:
The International Conference on Systems Engineering Research (CSER) is the primary conference for research focused on the fast-evolving systems engineering discipline and associated engineering practices. It has become a global platform for creative research in systems engineering. It addresses systems engineering research that is focused on the complexity of modern cyber-physical systems and the context within which they provide value to society. CSER was co-founded by systems faculty leaders at Stevens Institute of Technology and the University of Southern California in 2003; accordingly, CSER 2023 was the 20th edition of this venerable research conference series. Since its inception, CSER has become the primary conference for disseminating systems engineering research; germinating new research ideas; and nucleating new collaborative initiatives between academics and practitioners across the systems research and practice landscape.
The CSER 2023 theme emphasizes the pivotal role of a transdisciplinary systems engineering research community in conceiving and creating smart systems and the transition toward a more sustainable, safe and secure society. Smart systems are systems that apply some combination of artificial intelligence, machine learning, digitalization and data analytics to provide performance enhancements, generate automated insights and enable informed decisions. Modern systems, which have profound impacts on economic, environmental and social sustainability create complex challenges that demand a transdisciplinary approach. These CSER 2023 proceedings feature 47 chapters, authored by researchers from around the globe, covering foundational and cutting-edge topics in systems engineering research, including Artificial Intelligence for Systems and Software Engineering, Systems and Software Engineering for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Engineering, Digital Twins, Digital Transportation, Industry 4.0 and Lean Manufacturing, Model-Based Systems Engineering, Cybersecurity and System Security Engineering, Uncertainty and Complexity Management, Human-Systems Integration, Big Data and Analytics, Cyber-Physical Systems, and System Thinking. Researchers and practitioners in systems engineering will find substantial value in the CSER 2023 proceedings.

Author: Eneanya, Austin
Title: Configurational Alignment in Digital Innovation: How Technological Capabilities Interact for Sustainable Product–Market Fit Using the PVP Framework
Abstract Note: Achieving sustainable product-market fit (PMF) is hindered by" architectural blindness"—the tendency of current innovation frameworks to view technological infrastructure as a passive delivery tool rather than an active driver of value. To address this, this study introduces the Product Value Proposition (PVP) Framework, modeling PMF as the coupling of three nodes: Customer, Product, and Foundational (infrastructure). Analyzing 21 tech ventures, the research identifies a key failure mechanism: Architecturally Induced Innovation Latency (), where back-end rigidity bottleneck front-end iteration. Ultimately, digital success depends on coupling front-end customer value with back-end technical agility.

Author: Yan, Aoyang; Zhong, Hao; Song, Daohan; Jia, Li
Title: How do Programmers Fix Bugs as Workarounds?
Abstract Note: In software development, issue tracker systems are widely used to manage bug reports. In such a system, a bug report can be filed, diagnosed, assigned, and fixed. In the standard process, a bug can be resolved as fixed, invalid, duplicated or won’t fix. Although the above resolutions are well-defined and easy to understand, a bug report can end with a less known resolution, ie, workaround. Compared with other resolutions, the definition of workarounds is more ambiguous. Besides the problem that is reported in a bug report, the resolution of a workaround raises more questions. Some questions are important for users, especially those programmers who build their projects upon others (eg, libraries). Although some early studies have been conducted to analyze API workarounds, many research questions on workarounds are still open. For example, which bugs are resolved as workarounds? Why is a bug report resolved as workarounds? What are the repairs and impacts of workarounds? In this paper, we conduct the first empirical study to explore the above research questions. In particular, we analyzed 200 real workarounds that were collected from 81 Apache projects. Our results lead to eight findings and answers to all the above questions. For example, if bug reports are resolved as workarounds, their problems often either arise in external projects (40%) or reside in programming environments (23.5%). Although the problems of some workarounds (38.5%) reside in the project where they are reported, it is difficult to fix them fully and perfectly. Our findings are useful to understand workarounds, and to improve software projects and issue trackers.

Author: Hajiabadi, Hamideh; Hilbert, Lennart; Koziolek, Anne
Title: SEAA 2022

Author: Murre, Donald
Title: What doesn’t match matters more
Abstract Note:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve documents by positive relevance (how similar a document is to a query) and generate answers from whatever scores highest. This paradigm has no mechanism for representing what a document does not answer. We argue that this omission is the root cause of the most dangerous RAG failures: confident wrong answers in high-stakes domains.
We present evidence from legal, medical, and financial retrieval that positive-only scoring fails in three systematic ways:(1) it cannot distinguish topically similar but jurisdictionally inapplicable documents (scope failure);(2) it cannot distinguish related but categorically different concepts (sibling failure); and (3) it cannot distinguish current from superseded versions of a document (temporal failure). Each failure mode produces false positives that are invisible to the generation layer.

Author: Sculley, David; Holt, Gary; Golovin, Daniel; Davydov, Eugene; Phillips, Todd; Ebner, Dietmar; Chaudhary, Vinay; Young, Michael; Crespo, Jean-Francois; Dennison, Dan
Title: Hidden technical debt in machine learning systems
Abstract Note: Machine learning offers a fantastically powerful toolkit for building useful complexprediction systems quickly. This paper argues it is dangerous to think ofthese quick wins as coming for free. Using the software engineering frameworkof technical debt, we find it is common to incur massive ongoing maintenancecosts in real-world ML systems. We explore several ML-specific risk factors toaccount for in system design. These include boundary erosion, entanglement,hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, configurationissues, changes in the external world, and a variety of system-level anti-patterns.

Author: Zhang, Zejun; Yang, Yanming; Xia, Xin; Lo, David; Ren, Xiaoxue; Grundy, John
Title: Unveiling the mystery of API evolution in Deep Learning frameworks: a case study of TensorFlow 2
Abstract Note: API developers have been working hard to evolve APIs to provide more simple, powerful, and robust API libraries. Although API evolution has been studied for multiple domains, such as Web and Android development, API evolution for deep learning frameworks has not yet been studied. It is not very clear how and why APIs evolve in deep learning frameworks, and yet these are being more and more heavily used in industry. To fill this gap, we conduct a large-scale and in-depth study on the API evolution of Tensorflow 2, which is currently the most popular deep learning framework. We first extract 6,329 API changes by mining API documentation of Tensorflow 2 across multiple versions and mapping API changes into functional categories on the Tensorflow 2 framework to analyze their API evolution trends. We then investigate the key reasons for API changes by referring to multiple information sources, e.g., API documentation, commits and StackOverflow. Finally, we compare API evolution in non-deep learning projects to that of Tensorflow 2, and identify some key implications for users, researchers, and API developers.

Author: Buselli, Irene; López, Anna Pallarès; Jiménez, Eduard Martín; Anguita, Davide; Roli, Fabio; Oneto, Luca
Title: Mitigating Unfair Regression in Machine Learning Model Updates
Abstract Note: Machine learning systems often require updates for various reasons, such as the availability of new data or models and the need to optimize different technical or ethical metrics. Typically, these metrics reflect an average performance rather than sample-wise behavior. Indeed, improvements in metrics like accuracy can introduce negative flips, where the updated model makes errors that the previous model did not make. In certain applications, these negative flips can be perceived by developers or users as a regression in performance, contributing to the hidden technical debt of machine learning systems. Moreover, if the distribution of negative flips is biased with respect to some sensitive attribute (e.g., gender or race), it may be perceived as discrimination, termed unfair regression. In this paper we show, for the first time, the existence of the phenomenon of unfair regression and propose different ethical metrics to measure it. Additionally, we offer two mitigation strategies - one focused on modifying the learning algorithm and one focused on modifying the tuning phase - to address this issue. Our results on real-world datasets confirm the existence of the unfair regression phenomenon and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed mitigation strategies.

Author: Pasupuleti, Vinil; Songa, Srinivasateja; Gulkotwar, Nagesh; Allala, Shyalendar Reddy; Tyagi, Shrey
Title: Behavioral Regression Testing for Continuously Updated Machine Learning Models
Abstract Note: Machine learning models deployed in production are frequently updated or retrained, yet no structured regression testing approach exists for ML systems. Practice relies on aggregate metrics that mask localized behavioral regressions affecting specific input subpopulations. This paper presents BRT-ML, a framework for Behavioral Regression Testing of continuously updated ML models. BRT-ML introduces behavioral partitions of the input space and uses them to construct regression test suites stable across updates. A behavioral regression oracle combines partition-level flip rates, distributional shift tests, and invariant violation checks into a Regressed/Drifted/Consistent verdict before each deployment. A controlled empirical study demonstrates detection of silent regressions caused by training-data contamination (<0.25pp accuracy change) while correctly distinguishing them from benign hyperparameter updates.

Author: Kang, Tae-Hoon; Lee, Won-Seok; Baek, Myung-Sun; Bae, Byungjun; Song, Hyoung-Kyu
Title: Deep Learning-Based Bootstrap Detection Scheme for Digital Broadcasting System
Abstract Note: In the advanced television systems committee (ATSC) 3.0 system, the concept of flexibility is significant for supporting backward compatibility within the same ATSC 3.0 system. However, since the conventional bootstrap signal detection scheme is difficult to support the flexibility, the conventional bootstrap signal detection scheme should be newly designed according to the change of version. In this paper, a convolution neural network (CNN) model for bootstrap signal detection in ATSC 3.0 is proposed to maintain the flexibility of bootstrap. Additionally, for minimizing the loss of error performance of CNN-based bootstrap detection scheme, this paper proposes two dimensional alternate array to utilize the correlation of the adjacent bootstrap symbol and proposes the offline learning method using the bootstrap signal corrupted by noise to improve the error performance.

Author: Barzoki, Alireza Tavakkoli; Kontogiannis, Kostas
Title: Predicting Bug Inducing Commits Using Commit-State Transition Analysis
Abstract Note: Continuous software engineering promotes the use of a release-small, release-often deployment model, with a key focus on the shift-left approach, where quality is assessed as early as possible in the software development life-cycle. To effectively implement this shift-left strategy, developers need tools and techniques that can provide early warnings when a module may be entering a failure-prone state following certain edits. In this paper, we propose a fault-proneness detection framework that analyzes the evolution of quality and technical debt metrics as a system progresses from one commit to the next. This framework can be applied in real-time, as code is committed. Specifically, a metrics vector defines the state of each commit. Commit sequences then form a commit state transition model, which can be analyzed to identify transition paths most likely to lead to an imminent bug-inducing commit. Our approach has shown promising results when evaluated using the SonarQube Technical Debt open-source dataset.

Author: Patcas, Rares-Danut
Title: AI-Powered Issue Classification and Task Prioritization
Abstract Note: Maintaining high-quality code and efficiently managing software issues are critical aspects of modern software development. As software projects grow in complexity, developers face increasing challenges in handling technical debt, prioritizing tasks, and addressing issues effectively. To tackle these challenges, this project presents multiple AI-based models designed to classify SonarQube issues into fault-prone and non-fault-prone categories and to prioritize GitHub issues into three urgency levels: High, Medium, and Low priority. By leveraging machine learning models, the system automates these processes, significantly reducing manual workload while ensuring that the most critical issues receive timely attention. This project integrates data from both SonarQube and GitHub APIs, applying advanced classification and prioritization techniques. This approach not only enhances issue management but also contributes to improving overall software quality by helping developers focus on the most impactful problems first.

Author: Avila-Campos, Pablo; Haxhibeqiri, Jetmir; Girmay, Merkebu; Moerman, Ingrid; Hoebeke, Jeroen
Title: Residual Service Time Optimization for legacy Wireless-TSN end nodes
Abstract Note: The emergence of Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) has enabled network determinism to a new level, offering high reliability and bounded latency for critical communications. However, the unpredictable nature of traffic generation also poses new challenges to TSN. While TSN is designed to maintain backward compatibility with the 802.1 standards, many end nodes may not be equipped to understand TSN. This can result in a less deterministic TSN, and suboptimal resource utilization, mainly driven by Residual Service Time (RST). To address these challenges, this study proposes three scheduling mechanisms to reduce RST: q-learning, active time slot update, and polynomial forecasting. Real-world data captured from our wireless-TSN (W-TSN) evaluation kit is used to compare the proposed approaches in terms of one-way latency. The results show that the machine learning approach outperforms the other methods in terms of overall latency. However, it is less effective in identifying the optimal time slot position compared to the other methods.

Author: Cherladine, Karthick; Rallabandi, Bhaskara Raju
Title: 5G Cybersecurity Paradigm: Quantum Computing Threats and Artificial Intelligence-Driven Defenses
Abstract Note: The integration of \mathbf5 G, AI, and quantum computing not only opened up great new possibilities but also made the security situation even more complicated with the introduction of new security challenges. The paper in question goes in-depth about the massive shift in 5G security that quantum computing is going to cause by making the classical encryption methods like RSA and ECC insecure, which would then lead to revealing encryption for network slices, authentication, and identity management. The authors through quantitative simulations as well as the synthesis of the literature create a matrix of the probability and impact of quantum attacks against the AI-based models’ like LSTM-RNN, Graph Neural Networks, and Federated Learning defensive capabilities. The cost-benefit and policy analysis results hint that moving to quantum-proof methods, particularly those that use latticebased cryptography, is a long-term investment that is worthwhile in terms of strength. In addition to this, the paper does not forget to mention the ethical concerns, the international standardization efforts, and the future of Quantum Machine Learning in active threat detection. The long-term transition to post-quantum methods demonstrated measurable improvements in security and operational stability during simulated deployments. Lastly, the proposal presents tactical recommendations for the establishment of quantum-secure, transparent, and compatible 5 G ecosystems.

Author: Ehsani, Ramtin; Rawal, Shriya; Cai, Yuanfang; Chatterjee, Preetha
Title: Faster Code, Deeper Debt? A Multivocal Literature Review on Technical Debt and Its Early Signs in LLM-Assisted Software Development
Abstract Note: With the rapid adoption of LLM-assisted coding, the need to manage the technical debt these systems introduce has become urgent. In this paper, we conduct a multivocal literature review of 104 sources (31 formal, 73 grey) to examine how LLM-assisted development contributes to technical debt and what strategies, metrics, and benchmarks exist to mitigate it. We find that LLMs often amplify traditional forms of technical debt, particularly code, design, and documentation debts, while also introducing new LLM-specific debts. Notably, we identify fast-integration debt, where rapidly generated code prioritizes speed over quality, triggering a domino effect that leads to governance debt and increased long-term maintenance costs. Additional emerging categories include prompt, ethical, data, and provenance debt, reflecting new challenges unique to LLM adoption. To address these, strategies suggested in the literature include human-in-the-loop frameworks, prompt engineering, and data quality alignment. In practice, tools such as SonarQube are commonly used to detect technical debt indicators, while research prototypes such as CodeSmellEval are emerging to assess how LLMs contribute to debts. However, no standardized benchmarks or LLM-specific metrics yet exist, leaving an important gap. Based on findings, we outline insights and future directions to ensure reliable integration of LLMs into software engineering workflows.

Author: Wang, Chong; Huang, Kaifeng; Zhang, Jian; Feng, Yebo; Zhang, Lyuye; Liu, Yang; Peng, Xin
Title: LLMs Meet Library Evolution: Evaluating Deprecated API Usage in LLM-Based Code Completion
Abstract Note: Large language models (LLMs), pre-trained or fine-tuned on large code corpora, have shown effectiveness in generating code completions. However, in LLM-based code completion, LLMs may struggle to use correct and up-to-date Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) due to the rapid and continuous evolution of libraries. While existing studies have highlighted issues with predicting incorrect APIs, the specific problem of deprecated API usage in LLM-based code completion has not been thoroughly investigated. To address this gap, we conducted the first evaluation study on deprecated API usage in LLM-based code completion. This study involved seven advanced LLMs, 145 API mappings from eight popular Python libraries, and 28,125 completion prompts. The study results reveal the status quo (i.e., API usage plausibility and deprecated usage rate) of deprecated API and replacing API usage in LLM-based code completion from the perspectives of model, prompt, and library, and indicate the root causes behind. Based on these findings, we propose two lightweight fixing approaches, ReplaceAPI and InsertPrompt, which can serve as baseline approaches for future research on mitigating deprecated API usage in LLM-based completion. Additionally, we provide implications for future research on integrating library evolution with LLM-driven software development.

Author: Lin, Guancheng; Yu, Xiao; Keung, Jacky; Hu, Xing; Xia, Xin; Liu, Alex X.
Title: Don’t Use a Cannon to Kill a Fly: Lightweight Model Editing for LLMs to Correct Deprecated API Recommendations
Abstract Note: Pre-trained or fine-tuned on large code corpora, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in code completion tasks. However, their embedded knowledge is constrained by the timeliness of training data, which often includes code using deprecated APIs. Consequently, LLMs frequently generate deprecated APIs that will no longer be supported in future versions of third-party libraries. While retraining LLMs on updated codebases could refresh their API knowledge, this approach is computationally expensive. Recently, lightweight model editing methods have emerged to efficiently correct specific knowledge in LLMs. However, it remains unclear whether these methods can effectively update deprecated API knowledge and enable edited models to generate up-to-date APIs. To address this gap, we conduct the first systematic study applying 10 state-of-the-art model editing techniques to update deprecated API knowledge in three LLMs: Qwen2.5-Coder, CodeGemma, and DeepSeek-Coder. We introduce EDAPIBench, a dedicated benchmark featuring over 70 deprecated APIs from 8 popular Python libraries, with more than 3,000 editing instances. Our results show that the parameter-efficient fine-tuning method AdaLoRA achieves the best performance in enabling edited models to generate correct, up-to-date APIs, but falls short in Specificity (i.e., the editing influences untargeted knowledge). To resolve this, we propose AdaLoRA-L, which defines “Common API Layers” (layers within the LLMs with high importance across all APIs, storing general knowledge and excluded from editing) and restricts edits exclusively to “Specific API Layers” (layers with high importance only for the target API, storing the API-specific knowledge). Experimental results demonstrate that AdaLoRA-L significantly improves Specificity while maintaining comparable performance across other evaluation metrics. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).
